items.title: Background
items.text: New to graph-based intrusion detection? This page covers the concepts used throughout the documentation: the two kinds of data that PIDSMaker turns into graphs, system provenance and network events, and how detectors learn from these graphs to find attacks.

items.title: Two views of an enterprise
items.text:
Attacks leave traces at two levels. Inside each host, the operating system can record what processes do: which files they read and write, which programs they run, which connections they open. Between hosts, the network and the authentication services record who connects to whom. PIDSMaker builds a graph from either view, and runs the same pipeline on both:

Provenance Network Records System events of a host, from audit frameworks (Linux Audit, ETW) or EDR telemetry Authentications and network flows between hosts Nodes Processes, files and netflows Hosts Edges System calls (EVENT_READ, EVENT_EXECUTE...) Authentications (LogOn, LogOff...) or flows (FLOW_START) Node features Text labels: paths, command lines, IPs and ports Host identity Edge features Event type Event type and attributes: logon type, ports, protocol, size... Detectors Provenance-based IDSs (PIDSs): Velox, Orthrus, Kairos... Network IDSs (NIDSs): Euler, Argus, LARES... Typical attacks Exploitation, implants, privilege escalation, exfiltration on a host Lateral movement across the hosts of a network Ground truth Attack nodes, in ground-truth files Malicious events, labelled in the database Datasets DARPA TC, OpTC, ATLASv2, CARBANAKv2 LANL, OpTC network flows

Both views are complementary: provenance shows in detail how a host was compromised, the network shows how an attacker moves between hosts. In PIDSMaker, most detectors designed for one view run on the other.

items.title: Provenance graphs
items.text:
System provenance is a detailed record of the activity of a computer system. Operating systems can be configured to capture it with their audit frameworks, such as Linux Audit or Event Tracing for Windows (ETW). It captures:

  • Process execution: which programs ran, with which arguments.
  • File operations: reads, writes, creations, deletions.
  • Network activity: connections and data transfers.
  • Inter-process communication: pipes, signals, shared memory.

Raw provenance logs are turned into a provenance graph: a directed graph whose nodes are system entities and whose edges are the interactions between them, with a timestamp.

graph LR
    nginx(["process: nginx"]) -- READ --> conf["file: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf"]
    nginx -- CONNECT --> sock{{"netflow: 10.0.0.5:8080"}}
    nginx -- CLONE --> sh(["process: sh"])
    sh -- EXECUTE --> curl["file: /usr/bin/curl"]

items.title: Node types
items.text:
Provenance datasets have three node types, each described by a textual label:

Type Entity Label attributes subject Processes and threads Executable path, command line file Files and directories File path netflow Network connections Remote IP address and port

The attributes used in each label are set with construction.node_label_features.

items.title: Edge types
items.text:
Edges represent system calls or events. The DARPA TC datasets use 10 edge types:

Edge type Description EVENT_READ A process reads from a file EVENT_WRITE A process writes to a file EVENT_OPEN A process opens a file EVENT_EXECUTE A process executes a file EVENT_CONNECT A process connects to a remote host EVENT_RECVFROM A process receives network data EVENT_RECVMSG A process receives a network message EVENT_SENDTO A process sends network data EVENT_SENDMSG A process sends a network message EVENT_CLONE A process creates a child process (fork)

OpTC and the Carbon Black EDR datasets (ATLASv2, CARBANAKv2) have their own event types.

items.title: Network graphs
items.text:
Network logs record the communications between the hosts of a network: authentications of a user from one computer to another, or flows of packets between two addresses. They are turned into a network graph: a directed graph whose nodes are hosts and whose edges are these events, with a timestamp and attributes.

graph LR
    c1(["host: C1065"]) -- "LogOn · Network · NTLM" --> c2(["host: C586"])
    c1 -- "LogOn · Network · NTLM" --> c3(["host: C625"])
    c3 -- "LogOff" --> c2

There is a single node type, host, identified by its name or ID. Edge types and attributes depend on the dataset:

Dataset Edge types Edge attributes LANL Orientation of the authentication: LogOn, LogOff, TGS, TGT, AuthMap, ScreenLock, ScreenUnlock (and FLOW, if the flows are loaded) Logon type, authentication type, success, kinds of source and destination users (ports, protocol, duration, packets and bytes of flows) OPTC_NET FLOW_START (default), FLOW_MESSAGE Source and destination ports, protocol, size

construction.edge_type can use a categorical attribute as edge type instead, e.g. logon_type. All of them are defined in the dataset's schema (pidsmaker/config/schemas.py).

Unlike the entities of provenance graphs, hosts have no descriptive label: network detectors learn an embedding of the identity of each host, and rely on the attributes of its events.

items.title: How graph-based IDSs detect attacks
items.text:
Labeled attacks are rare, so both PIDSs and NIDSs use self-supervised learning: they learn what normal activity looks like, then flag what deviates from it.

1. Training, on benign data only

flowchart LR
    A[Benign events] --> B[Graph construction] --> C[GNN encoder] --> D[Model of normal behavior]

2. Detection, on test data with attacks

flowchart LR
    E[Test events] --> F[Predictions of the trained model] --> G{Error above threshold?}
    G -- yes --> H[Malicious]
    G -- no --> I[Benign]

Training. The model learns the patterns of normal behavior from benign activity, with a self-supervised task:

ProvenanceNetwork

Which processes access which files, how they communicate over the network, which events usually follow each other. PIDSs learn to predict the type of each edge (Velox, Orthrus, Kairos), the type of each node (Flash, ThreaTrace) or to reconstruct node features (MAGIC, NodLink).

Which hosts usually authenticate to or connect with which others, and how. NIDSs learn to tell real edges from random ones (link prediction: Euler, Argus, Jbeil, E-GraphSAGE), or to reconstruct the embeddings of edges (LARES).

Detection. On the test data, the trained model makes the same predictions. A high error means that the behavior was not seen in training: an entity that suddenly reads unusual files, or a host that logs on to computers it never contacted. Nodes, edges or time windows whose error exceeds a threshold, chosen on validation data, are flagged as malicious.

items.title: How detection is evaluated
items.text:
Detections are compared with the ground truth of the dataset, at the granularity that fits each view:

  • Provenance detectors are usually evaluated per node: is each process, file or netflow part of an attack? The ground truth lists the attack nodes of each attack.
  • Network detectors are usually evaluated per edge: is each authentication or flow malicious? The ground truth is the label of each event. LARES first selects the most suspicious hosts, then their most suspicious edges.

Because attacks are tiny compared to benign activity, metrics that don't depend on a threshold (AUC, AP) and attack-centric metrics (how many attacks are detected, with how many false positives) matter as much as precision and recall. See Evaluation & labeling.

items.title: Graph neural networks
items.text:
Most systems in PIDSMaker use graph neural networks (GNNs), neural networks designed for graph-structured data.

GNNs work by message passing: at each layer, every node aggregates information from its neighbors to update its representation. After k layers, the embedding of a node captures its k-hop neighborhood: below, A learns about its neighbors B and C after one layer, and about D and E, two hops away, after two.

graph LR
    D((D)) --> B((B)) --> A((A))
    E((E)) --> C((C)) --> A

Graphs change over time, so systems either embed each time window independently, or carry information across windows: a temporal memory of each node (TGN, in Kairos, Orthrus and Jbeil) or a recurrent network over the successive embeddings of each node (Euler, Argus).

PIDSMaker provides many GNN encoders (GraphSAGE, GAT, GCN, TGN, RGCN, graph transformers...) and self-supervised objectives (edge type prediction, node type prediction, feature reconstruction, link prediction...), which can be combined freely.

items.title: Takeaways
items.text:
• Every run completes, with 1 TB of RAM and an 80 GB GPU.
  • A large GPU is not needed: no run uses more than 32 GB of GPU memory, and 88 of 97 stay under 12 GB.
  • Network systems other than Jbeil are the cheapest: under 30 minutes outside TRACE_E3. They merge repeated edges and skip text embeddings.
  • Jbeil is the slowest: 2.5 to 7.8 hours on all datasets but CADETS_E3, 85 to 97% of it training its TGN on batches of 200 edges. Training is also 69 to 88% of the time of Kairos, Orthrus and Velox.
  • ProGrapher's time goes to graph2vec, 77 to 98% of it: 174 minutes on THEIA_E5 and 200 on TRACE_E3.
  • TRACE_E3 is the most expensive dataset: 34 to 113 minutes for most systems, 28 GB of RAM for the median one and up to 102 GB (NodLink). Elsewhere, no run needs more than 40 GB of RAM.
  • Per-epoch outputs fill the disk: 24 of the 30 GB of Euler on THEIA_E5. --keep_best_epoch_only keeps only those of the reported epoch.

items.title: PROVENANCE_BENIGN
items.text:
A Linux audit corpus used only to pretrain SPIDER. It has no ground truth, so it can't be used to evaluate detection. It is downloaded like the other datasets (pidsmaker download PROVENANCE_BENIGN, 2 MB).

It is built on a Linux machine: auditd records the system calls of 21 scripted workloads (from core utilities, compilers and package managers to web servers, databases, browsers and attack-like commands), the logs are parsed into entities and edges, and create_database_provenance_benign.py loads them into a PROVENANCE_BENIGN database with the DARPA TC schema. The collection scripts are on the spider branch, and their README describes each step.

The dates of PROVENANCE_BENIGN in DATASET_DEFAULT_CONFIG (pidsmaker/config/config.py) are those of the corpus used in the paper (2026-03-16, UTC). Set them to the days of your own capture.

items.title: Network datasets
items.text:
Network datasets record the communications between the hosts of an enterprise network, authentications or flows, during benign activity and a red team campaign. Their single node type is the host, and their events carry attributes (logon types, ports, protocols, sizes...) that become edge features (batching.edge_features=edge_attrs). Both are described by a schema in pidsmaker/config/schemas.py, and both are built from the preprocessed files of LARES (see Building datasets from scratch).

Malicious events are labelled in the database (label column), so the ground truth is event-level: the evaluation labels each edge with its events. Models are trained and validated on benign events only: construction.benign_training (on by default) drops the malicious events of the train and val dates, which has no effect when they have none (as for LANL and OPTC_NET).

items.title: LANL
items.text:
The "Comprehensive, Multi-Source Cyber-Security Events" dataset of the Los Alamos National Laboratory: 58 days of authentications between the computers of the LANL network, with the red team events of a penetration test. As in Euler, Argus, Jbeil and LARES, only NTLM authentications are kept. Edges are authentications, typed by their orientation (LogOn, LogOff, ...), with the logon type, authentication type, success and kinds of source and destination users as attributes.

LANL timestamps are seconds from an undisclosed origin, mapped to UTC dates such that the first red team event happens on 2015-01-03. Models are trained on 2015-01-01, validated on 2015-01-02 and tested from 2015-01-03 to 2015-01-30. The root source of the attack is host 9660.

pidsmaker SYSTEM LANL

items.title: OPTC_NET
items.text:
The network flows of all the hosts of DARPA OpTC (eCAR FLOW START and FLOW MESSAGE events), from 2019-09-16 to 2019-09-25. Edges are flows, with the source and destination ports (grouped by service and range), the protocol and the size of messages as attributes. As in LARES and Argus, only FLOW START events are used by default (construction.operations). Models are trained from 2019-09-16 to 2019-09-21, validated on 2019-09-22 and tested from 2019-09-23 to 2019-09-25 (malicious flows happen on 2019-09-23 and 2019-09-24). The root sources of the attacks are hosts 201, 402 and 501.

LARES labels only some of the records of each malicious flow (a flow has FLOW START and FLOW MESSAGE events, recorded by the hosts at both ends). By default, the database labels malicious all the records of a malicious flow (same 5-tuple in the same LARES file): 1,015 malicious FLOW START events instead of the 115 of LARES. The labels of LARES are kept by building the database with --no_label_propagation (see Building datasets from scratch, tab OpTC flows)). Euler and Argus use another preprocessing and labelling of OpTC (IP addresses as nodes, including external hosts, and all the events of compromised hosts as malicious), so their results on OpTC are not comparable.

99.9% of the FLOW START events are NetBIOS, LLMNR and SSDP broadcasts and multicasts and ICMPv6 neighbor discovery, which link each host to most hosts in every time window. They are dropped by default (construction.drop_noise_events, which has no effect on other datasets); set construction.drop_noise_events=False to keep them, as LARES does. The OpTC hyperparameters of LARES (30 min windows, α = 5, β = 30) and the 6 min snapshots of Argus are loaded with --tuned (config/tuned_baselines/optc_net/).

pidsmaker SYSTEM OPTC_NET

items.title: Train, validation and test splits
items.text:
Each dataset is split by day, as defined by train_dates, val_dates and test_dates in DATASET_DEFAULT_CONFIG (pidsmaker/config/config.py):

  • Train days: benign activity only, used to train the model.
  • Validation days: benign activity only, used to pick the detection threshold.
  • Test days: benign activity and attacks, used for evaluation.

On datasets with labelled events, construction.benign_training enforces it by dropping the malicious events of the train and validation days.

The events of each day are then cut into time-window graphs during construction.

items.title: Ground truth
items.text:
The two kinds of datasets are labelled differently:

  • Provenance datasets come with the list of the nodes involved in each attack, in files under ground_truth/. PIDSMaker ships several labelings of the DARPA TC attacks (orthrus, reapr, threatrace).
  • Network datasets label their events in the database. Malicious nodes are the endpoints of malicious events.

See Ground truth for how they are selected and how labels are assigned to nodes, edges and time windows.

To add a new dataset, define its configuration in pidsmaker/config/config.py:

DATASET_DEFAULT_CONFIG = {
    "MY_DATASET": {
        "raw_dir": "",

Then follow the database creation guide to load your data, and add its ground truth under ground_truth/ (or, with a schema that has a label column, label its events in the database, as the network datasets). A dataset with labelled events, like LANL, sets ground_truth_relative_path and attack_to_time_window to empty lists, and can set root_attack_nodes, the root sources of its attacks used by the host-centered evaluation.

items.title: Evaluation & labeling
items.text: The same detector can look excellent or useless depending on what is counted as a detection, how it is labeled, and which threshold is used. This page explains each of these choices in PIDSMaker, for provenance and network datasets, so that results can be compared fairly.

items.title: From losses to metrics
items.text:
1. Losses. After training, the model computes a loss for every edge (or node, for node-level objectives) of the validation and test graphs. This is done at epoch 0 and then every two epochs, and saved per time window.
  2. Scores. The evaluation method groups the losses into the samples it classifies (nodes, edges, time windows...) and reduces them into one anomaly score per sample.
  3. Threshold. A threshold is computed from the validation losses, which contain benign activity only. Samples scoring above it are predicted malicious.
  4. Labels. Each sample gets a ground-truth label, derived from the list of attack nodes of provenance datasets, or from the labels of the events of network datasets.
  5. Metrics. Predictions are compared with the labels, for each evaluated epoch, and the metrics of the best epoch are reported.

The evaluation method is set with evaluation.used_method, and its options in the sub-section of the same name. Each family has its usual granularity, which evaluation.used_method changes for any system:

Provenance systems Network systems Default evaluation node_evaluation: is each process, file or netflow part of an attack? edge_evaluation: is each authentication or flow malicious? host_two_stage_evaluation for LARES: which hosts are the sources of the attack, and which of their edges are malicious? Ground truth Attack nodes, in ground-truth files Malicious events, labelled in the database Reported epoch Best ADP (best_adp) Chosen without labels (best_val_score, last_epoch), or best MCC for LARES

See the settings of each system.

items.title: Evaluation granularities
items.text:
The ground truth lists attack nodes (provenance datasets) or malicious events (network datasets). Each evaluation method turns it into labels for the unit it classifies:

TW1TW2TW3same node = 1 sampleNode node_evaluationOne sample per node over the whole test set. Its score is the max loss of its edges in all windows. Malicious if the node is in the ground truth. TW1TW2TW3same node = 2 samplesNode × time window node_tw_evaluationOne sample per (node, window) pair: the same node in two windows counts twice. Malicious if the node is malicious in that window. TW1TW2TW3each edge = 1 sampleEdge edge_evaluationOne sample per event, scored by its own loss. Malicious if its source, destination or both are attack nodes, as set by malicious_edge_selection. TW1TW2TW3each window = 1 sampleTime window tw_evaluationOne sample per time-window graph, scored by reducing the losses of its edges. Malicious if it contains at least one attack event. TW1TW2TW3TW2 + TW3 = 1 queueQueue queue_evaluationKairos: anomalous windows that share rare nodes are chained into a queue. All windows of a queue whose score exceeds queue_threshold are flagged. benign nodeattack node (ground truth)one sample, labeled benignone sample, labeled malicious evaluation.used_method Sample Score Label: malicious if... node_evaluation A node, over the whole test set Max (or mean, or 95th percentile) of the losses of its edges, as source (and as destination with use_dst_node_loss) the node is in the ground truth node_tw_evaluation A (node, time window) pair Same reduction, over the node's losses in that window the node is an attack node of that window edge_evaluation An edge (event) The loss of the edge its source, destination or both are attack nodes, during an attack (malicious_edge_selection: src_node, dst_node, both_nodes); on network datasets, one of its events is labelled malicious tw_evaluation A time-window graph Reduction of all the losses of the window it contains at least one attack event queue_evaluation A time-window graph, through its queue Score of the queue that contains it it contains at least one attack event host_two_stage_evaluation An edge, predicted by the top-scored hosts The loss of the edge as edge_evaluation with both_nodes, or its event label (see below)

Which samples are evaluated?

Only samples seen during inference are evaluated: a node that never appears in the test graphs is neither scored nor counted as a false negative. Empty time windows are skipped.

node_tw_evaluation is closer to real-time detection: an alert must happen in the window of the attack, and a node that is benign most of the time and malicious in one window counts as one true positive and several true negatives.

items.title: Queues (Kairos)
items.text:
queue_evaluation with used_method: kairos_idf_queue reproduces the detection of Kairos, which requires edge-level losses:

  1. In each test window, edges with a loss above the window's mean + 1.5 × std are anomalous. The window's loss is the mean loss of these edges.
  2. Windows are chained into queues when they share a rare node, measured by its IDF over the graphs (network nodes are ignored). include_test_set_in_IDF also counts the test graphs.
  3. The score of a queue is the product of (loss + 1) over its windows. All windows of queues scoring above queue_threshold are flagged.

The provnet_lof_queue method is not supported anymore.

items.title: Host-centered evaluation (LARES)
items.text:
host_two_stage_evaluation reproduces the two-stage evaluation of LARES, on edge-level losses:

  1. Each host is scored by the maximum loss of its outgoing edges over the test period. The alpha highest host scores are split into two clusters with k-means, and the hosts of the high-score cluster are selected, along with the host ranked just below them.
  2. The beta highest-scored outgoing edges of each selected host are predicted malicious.

With root_attack_nodes, only the malicious edges of these source hosts are positives, as in LARES (dataset uses the root sources of the dataset: 9660 on LANL, 201,402,501 on OPTC_NET). test_end ends the evaluated period earlier (LARES evaluates LANL on its first 14 days). Precision, recall and MCC come from the predictions of the two stages, AUC and AP from the edge losses; the rank of each root host is also reported. No threshold is used.

items.title: Ground truth
items.text:
Evaluation compares predictions against a ground truth. For provenance datasets, it is the UUIDs of the nodes involved in each attack, described below; network datasets label their events instead (event-level labels). The labeling of the DARPA TC attacks differs between prior works, and the choice of ground truth materially affects the reported metrics, so PIDSMaker ships several, selected with evaluation.ground_truth_version (default orthrus):

CLIYAML 
pidsmaker SYSTEM CADETS_E3 --evaluation.ground_truth_version threatrace

evaluation:
  ground_truth_version: threatrace
Version Source Format Coverage orthrus (default) Labeling used by Orthrus One CSV per attack, rows of uuid, {labels}, count All provenance datasets reapr Alternative labeling of the DARPA TC E3 datasets Same as orthrus E3: CADETS, THEIA, TRACE, FIVEDIRECTIONS threatrace Ground truth published by ThreaTrace One flat UUID-per-line .txt per dataset, treated as a single attack over the whole test period E3: CADETS, THEIA, TRACE, FIVEDIRECTIONS

The files live under ground_truth/<version>/<dataset>/. Changing the version only changes the labels read by evaluation: it doesn't change training or the graphs, so it re-evaluates an already-trained run.

  • Attacks. Each dataset defines its attacks in attack_to_time_window (DATASET_DEFAULT_CONFIG, pidsmaker/config/config.py): one ground-truth file and one time range per attack. Attacks are what ADP and the per-attack metrics count.
  • Node labels. A node is malicious if it appears in any attack file. UUIDs of the ground truth that are not in the graphs are skipped, and counted in the logs.
  • Window labels. A time window is malicious if it contains a database event, inside an attack's time range, whose source or destination is an attack node.

Selecting a version that has no file for the dataset fails with a clear error. See ground_truth/threatrace/README.md for the per-dataset ThreaTrace node counts.

items.title: Event-level labels (network datasets)
items.text: Datasets whose schema has a label column, such as LANL and OPTC_NET, label their events in the database instead of shipping ground-truth files, and ground_truth_version has no effect on them. Edges carry the labels of their events (also after merge_edges), malicious nodes are the endpoints of malicious events, and, as these datasets define no attack_to_time_window, all malicious events form a single attack over the test period.

items.title: Thresholds
items.text:
threshold_method (in the section of the evaluation method) sets both how losses are reduced into a score and how the threshold is computed. Thresholds are computed on the validation losses unless stated otherwise.

threshold_method Score of a sample Threshold Used by max_val_loss Max loss Max validation loss × alpha (node_evaluation.max_val_loss.alpha, node and edge evaluation only) Velox, Orthrus, Kairos, R-Caid, network systems except LARES mean_val_loss Mean loss Mean validation loss percentile 95th percentile of the losses Max validation loss × alpha nodlink Max loss 90th percentile of the validation losses NodLink threatrace Max over time windows of log(1.5) − log(p_true/p_other), where p_true is the probability of the true node type and p_other the highest of the others; with training.used_method: threatrace, the min over the submodels 0: flagged unless a model predicts the true node type with a probability ratio above 1.5 ThreaTrace flash Max over time windows of 1 − c if the node type is predicted correctly and 1 + c otherwise, with c = (p₁ − p₂)/p₁ on the node type probabilities, min-max normalized per window. With predict_node_type.flash_snapshots, the min over the snapshots of the epochs so far Flagged unless predicted correctly with c > 0.53 (score ≥ 0.47) Flash magic Max over time windows of the mean distance to the magic_knn_k (10) nearest benign training embeddings, divided by the mean k-NN distance of the training nodes Mean score over the test nodes MAGIC ocrapt Max loss Per node type: the top fraction of scores, set by ocrapt_contamination and ocrapt_min_contamination OCR-APT fixed_zero Max loss 0 (decision boundary of a binary classifier) Supervised objective

threatrace and flash require the predict_node_type objective, and magic requires node-level evaluation with a node-level objective.

With node-level objectives, the scores of threatrace, flash and magic are computed at inference, and each node is flagged at evaluation, by the NodeScorer of the system (in pidsmaker/detection/threatrace_detection.py, flash_detection.py and magic_knn.py). A new threshold method with scores of its own subclasses NodeScorer (pidsmaker/detection/node_scoring.py) and registers it in node_scorer_factory() (factory.py).

items.title: Clustering (Orthrus)
items.text: With use_kmeans: True, the threshold doesn't decide alone: the kmeans_top_K highest-scored nodes are split into two clusters with k-means on their scores, and only the nodes of the high-score cluster are predicted malicious. With node_tw_evaluation, clustering runs in each window that has at least one node above the threshold. The original Orthrus enables it with K = 30; PIDSMaker's orthrus disables it to avoid data snooping.

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
Every evaluation method reports the standard classification metrics, computed from the predictions (above the threshold) or directly from the scores:

Metric Meaning precision, recall, fscore, fpr, mcc, accuracy, balanced_acc Classification metrics of the thresholded predictions tp, fp, tn, fn Confusion matrix ap, auc Average precision and ROC AUC of the scores: they don't depend on the threshold precision@K, recall@K, ap@K The same, among the K highest-scored samples (K = 10, 50, 100)

Node and edge evaluation also report attack-centric metrics. They matter because attacks are tiny compared to benign activity: detecting one node of each attack with few false positives is often more useful than a high recall.

adp_score Attack Detection Precision. Samples are ranked by score. At each rank, PIDSMaker computes the precision and the percentage of attacks with at least one detected node. ADP is the area under the curve of the attacks detected against precision: 1.0 means that every attack is detected before any false positive. discrimination For each attack, the gap between its highest score and the mean of the 10 highest benign scores (scores normalized by their max), averaged over attacks. Positive when attacks stand out from the most suspicious benign nodes. *_if_all_attacks_detected The precision, recall, TPs and FPs obtained with the lowest threshold that still detects every attack. percent_detected_attacks, tp_att_<i> The fraction of attacks detected by the threshold, and the true positives of each attack (node evaluation).

items.title: Choosing the reported epoch
items.text:
Every evaluated epoch is logged, and the metrics of the best one are reported, as selected by evaluation.best_model_selection:

Value Best epoch best_adp (default) Highest ADP, ties broken by discrimination best_discrimination Highest discrimination best_ap@10 Highest AP among the 10 highest scores, ties broken by discrimination best_mcc Highest MCC, as in the code of LARES best_val_score Highest score on validation data computed by the objective, without labels: the AUC + AP of link prediction on the validation edges with predict_edge_contrastive (Euler's early stopping) last_epoch Last evaluated epoch, without labels

With best_adp, best_discrimination and best_ap@10, time-window evaluations, which have no ADP, use the highest AP. Queue evaluation uses the highest precision, then recall.

With a label-free selection (best_val_score or last_epoch), evaluation.evaluate_selected_epoch_only=True evaluates only the selected epoch on the test set, instead of every epoch: faster on large test sets, but without per-epoch test metrics.

Most selections use test metrics

best_adp, best_discrimination, best_ap@10 and best_mcc select the epoch on the metrics of the test set. Keep this in mind when comparing with systems that select their model on validation data only (best_val_score, last_epoch), and evaluate over several runs.

items.title: Outputs
items.text:
Results are written to the precision_recall_dir/ folder of the evaluation task, for each epoch: the scores and predictions (scores_*.pkl, result_*.pth, stats_*.pth) and figures, also sent to W&B:

  • scores_*.png and neat_scores_*.svg: the score of every node, with attack nodes highlighted and the threshold.
  • adp_curve_*.png: the curve whose area is the ADP.
  • discrim_curve_*.png and distrib_*.png: the distribution of scores per node type.

Figures with one point per node or edge are slow to draw on large test sets: evaluation.save_figures=False skips them, and the metrics are computed either way. The network systems disable them by default.

items.title: Pipeline
items.text:
PIDSMaker breaks every system, provenance-based or network, into the same seven stages. Each stage is configured by a section of the system's YAML file in config/, so building a new system amounts to picking a method, and its arguments, for each stage.

items.title: The stages
items.text:
1. Construction (construction): reads the events of the dataset from its database (Parquet files, queried with DuckDB), optionally cleans them, and builds one graph per time window (e.g. 15 minutes). The dataset's schema (pidsmaker/config/schemas.py) defines its node types, edge types and event attributes.
  2. Transformation (transformation): optional transformations of the graphs, applied in sequence: making them undirected, turning them into DAGs, building the R-Caid pseudo-graph, merging repeated edges into weighted edges (merge_edges), or injecting synthetic attacks.
  3. Featurization (featurization, then feat_inference): learns a text embedding model on the labels of the entities (word2vec, doc2vec, FastText, hierarchical hashing, a pretrained encoder...) and embeds every node, or uses label-free features (only_type, only_ones). The attributes of events, if the dataset has any, are encoded as edge features.
  4. Batching (batching): selects the node and edge features, and builds the batches given to the model: global, intra-graph and inter-graph batching, TGN neighbor sampling.
  5. Training (training): trains the encoder and the self-supervised objective on benign graphs, then computes the losses on the validation and test graphs.
  6. Evaluation (evaluation): turns losses into anomaly scores, picks a threshold on the validation set, and computes the metrics at the node, edge, time-window, queue or host level. See Evaluation & labeling.
  7. Triage (triage): optional post-processing of node-level detections, to reconstruct attack paths (DepImpact) or anomalous subgraphs (OCR-APT) and reduce false positives. See Triage.

The methods available at each stage, and all their arguments, are listed in the Reference.

items.title: Provenance and network views
items.text:
The same stages build provenance-based IDSs (PIDSs) and network IDSs (NIDSs). What changes is the data that flows through them, and the components that the systems of each family use by default:

Stage Provenance (e.g. Orthrus on CADETS_E3) Network (e.g. Euler or LARES on LANL) Construction System events between processes, files and netflows, typed by system call (EVENT_READ, EVENT_CONNECT...). Raw data can be cleaned. Authentications or flows between hosts, typed by their operation (LogOn, FLOW_START...) or by a categorical attribute (construction.edge_type=logon_type). construction.operations and construction.drop_noise_events select the events, and construction.benign_training drops the labelled malicious events of the train and val dates. Transformation Usually none; undirected (NodLink), rcaid_pseudo_graph (R-Caid). merge_edges: the repeated edges of a window become one edge weighted by its count, optionally with aggregated attributes (counts per value, mean and std). Featurization Text embeddings of the labels of entities: file paths, command lines, IP addresses and ports. Hosts only have a name or an ID (e.g. C1065 in LANL): NIDSs use only_type or only_ones, and learn the identity of each host in the encoder. Event attributes are encoded as edge features: one-hot categorical and log-scaled numeric attributes, selected with feat_inference.edge_attributes. Batching Node features node_emb,node_type; edge features edge_type or TGN messages. Edge features edge_attrs (Argus, LARES, E-GraphSAGE, Anomal-E). Training Predict the type of edges or nodes, or reconstruct node features. Link prediction against negative edges (predict_edge_contrastive), edge autoencoder, Deep Graph Infomax; host identity and snapshot encoders (node_id_embedding, snapshot_gru). Evaluation Per node, against the attack nodes listed in ground-truth files (node_evaluation). Per edge, against the malicious events labelled in the database (edge_evaluation), or host-centered (host_two_stage_evaluation). Epochs can be selected without labels (best_val_score, last_epoch). Triage DepImpact or OCR-APT subgraphs, from the detected nodes. Not used: triage starts from node-level detections, and NIDSs detect edges.

These are the defaults of each family, not restrictions: components work on both kinds of datasets, except those that need several node types or event attributes. See Running across families and the components of each system.

items.title: Caching of tasks
items.text:
PIDSMaker computes a hash for each task from its arguments and the arguments of all the tasks before it. When a task completes, its outputs are saved on disk in a folder named after this hash. On the next run, PIDSMaker recomputes the hashes: if a folder already exists, the task is skipped and its outputs are reused.

Example

Running the same config twice: the first run executes every task (if nothing was run before with these arguments); the second skips them all, since their outputs already exist.

Now change the text embedding size, featurization.emb_dim. The hashes of construction and transformation don't change, so their outputs are reused, and the pipeline resumes from featurization.

flowchart LR
    A[construction] --> B[transformation] --> C[featurization] --> D[feat_inference] --> E[batching] --> F[training] --> G[evaluation] --> H[triage]
    classDef cached fill:#e5602a22,stroke:#e5602a;
    class A,B cached;

With --featurization.emb_dim=64: the highlighted tasks are reused, the others run again.

This makes experiments much faster: tuning the learning rate never rebuilds the graphs.

Arguments added in new versions of PIDSMaker are left out of the hash while they keep their default value, so the outputs computed before they existed are still reused after an update.

Avoid concurrent runs with identical early tasks

If two runs with the same construction arguments and dataset start at the same time, they write to the same folder. Start the first run and wait until its shared tasks are done before launching the others, or use --restart_from_scratch.

items.title: Command line arguments
items.text:
YAML files set the default arguments of a system, and CLI arguments override them:

pidsmaker orthrus CADETS_E3 \
    --featurization.emb_dim=64 \
    --training.lr=0.0001

is equivalent to adding to the YAML config:

featurization:
  emb_dim: 64
training:
  lr: 0.0001

New systems can inherit from an existing one with _include_yml and override only what changes:

config/my_system.yml
_include_yml: magic

training:
  decoder:
    used_methods: predict_node_type
    predict_node_type:
      node_mlp:
        architecture_str: linear(0.5) | relu

evaluation:
  node_evaluation:
    threshold_method: nodlink

items.title: Forcing a restart
items.text:
During development, you may need to re-run tasks with the same arguments, for example after changing the code. --force_restart restarts the pipeline from a given task:

pidsmaker orthrus CADETS_E3 --force_restart=featurization

Note

A forced restart overwrites the outputs previously saved for the same tasks.

To run the whole pipeline without touching previous outputs, use:

pidsmaker orthrus CADETS_E3 --restart_from_scratch

The outputs are then written to a new folder named after a random hash, isolated from all previous runs.

Warning

Since the hash is random, these outputs can't be found again from the task arguments. All files produced with --restart_from_scratch are therefore deleted at the end of the run, to save disk space.

items.title: Performance
items.text:
The pipeline was optimized for speed and memory without changing its outputs: graphs, features, the batches given to the models, losses and metrics are identical to those of previous versions (GPU training is not bit-deterministic, so a few losses can differ by about 0.0001). Measured on full runs from scratch, before and after the optimizations:

Run Wall time Peak RAM Disk Orthrus, THEIA_E5 ~3.4 h → ~61 min 370 → 16.6 GB Orthrus, CADETS_E3 42 → 20 min 47 → 4.8 GB 9.7 → 2.2 GB Orthrus, optc_h201 95 → 29 min 128 → 11.1 GB 25.9 → 8.1 GB Kairos, CADETS_E3 72 → 30 min 14.4 → 4.7 GB 4.5 → 1.6 GB Kairos, optc_h501 191 → 39 min 37 → 10.0 GB 13.6 → 5.7 GB

Measured in PR #77; the CADETS_E3 and OpTC runs used A100 80 GB GPUs, and peak RAM is the resident memory of the largest process. On THEIA_E5, construction went from 824 to 204 s, feat_inference from 619 to 397 s, training (12 epochs) from 8,945 to 2,255 s and evaluation from 1,685 to 494 s.

On the network datasets (PR #78), merging the edges of the 205 graphs of OPTC_NET (LARES) went from ~77 to 4.5 min, the edge evaluation of one epoch (38M edges) from 658 to 58 s, and LARES on OPTC_NET end to end from more than 2 h to 15 min.

items.title: Parallel graph construction
items.text:
Graph construction builds the graphs of each day of the dataset in parallel processes. The number of processes is set with --num_workers (default: min(8, #CPUs)); it does not change the produced graphs, nor the task hashes.

pidsmaker orthrus CADETS_E3 --num_workers 16

The graphs of the time windows are also transformed in --num_workers parallel processes, including by the R-Caid pseudo-graph (rcaid_pseudo_graph), whose random timestamps are drawn in window order from the same random state as in a sequential run, so that the transformed graphs are unchanged. The R-Caid transformation itself computes the descendants of the roots once per distinct set of successors, stops exploring those of the roots that will be pruned, and saves its edges without building networkx graphs: on CADETS_E3, the transformation task went from 371 to 6.5 s with 4 processes, with identical graphs.

items.title: Shared node features
items.text:
During training, node features (embeddings and types) are stored once in a shared table, and each batch only holds node IDs: its features are rebuilt on the GPU when the batch is used, with the same operations as before, so the model receives identical inputs. This divides the RAM used by the loaded graphs by about 4-6x (on CADETS_E3, from 11.9 to 1.9 GB with Orthrus and from 5.6 to 1.4 GB with Kairos), for roughly 10% more time per epoch and about 1 GB of GPU memory. Configurations whose node features depend on the graph (only_ones, edges_distribution), heterogeneous graphs, inter-graph batching and multi-dataset training keep storing features per batch. --no_shared_node_features disables the table.

Deterministic dataset reads

Datasets are always read in the same order. Their Parquet files store the node tables in a fixed order and the events sorted by timestamp_rec, event_uuid, and DuckDB returns the rows in their stored order: graphs, features and batches do not change from one run to the next.

items.title: Disk usage
items.text:
Outputs are stored in compact formats, and all readers still accept the previous ones, so existing artifact folders keep working:

Output Format Reduction Graphs of construction and transformation Compressed column arrays instead of pickled networkx graphs ~5x smaller Node features of feat_inference Node feature rows and per-edge row indices instead of one message per edge 6.1 → 0.9 GB on CADETS_E3 Losses of each epoch Compressed .npz instead of .csv ~8x smaller Edge scores of the edge evaluation (edge_scores_*.pkl) int32 instead of int64 columns ~35% smaller

torch.load on a graph file still returns the identical networkx graph.

Evaluation also stores per-epoch pickles. To keep only the outputs of the best epoch once the pipeline has finished, use --keep_best_epoch_only. Stats and plots are kept for every epoch, but re-running evaluation afterwards only considers the kept epoch(s).

pidsmaker orthrus CADETS_E3 --keep_best_epoch_only

items.title: Systems
items.text: PIDSMaker reimplements state-of-the-art intrusion detection systems as YAML configs in config/: provenance-based IDSs (PIDSs), which detect attacks in the system events of hosts, and network IDSs (NIDSs), which detect them in the communications between hosts. All of them are described with the same components, so they can be compared side by side, any component can be swapped into any other system, and most systems run on both kinds of datasets.

items.text:

pidsmaker lares OPTC_NET --tuned   # OpTC hyperparameters of LARES

All systems are self-supervised and trained on benign data only. PIDSs flag the entities (processes, files, netflows) whose activity deviates from what they learned; NIDSs flag the authentications or flows that their model finds unlikely. E-GraphSAGE, originally a supervised edge classifier, is trained here with self-supervised link prediction like the other NIDSs. The header of each config describes the system and its differences with the original implementation.

items.title: Components at a glance
items.text:
How each system is configured at the main stages of the pipeline:

System Featurization Encoder Objective Evaluation Threshold Velox word2vec none (linear layer) predict_edge_type node_evaluation max_val_loss Orthrus word2vec tgn, graph_attention predict_edge_type node_evaluation max_val_loss + k-means Kairos hierarchical_hashing graph_attention, tgn predict_edge_type node_evaluation max_val_loss MAGIC only_type magic_gat reconstruct_masked_features, predict_masked_struct node_evaluation magic Flash flash sage predict_node_type node_evaluation flash R-Caid doc2vec rcaid_gat predict_process_tag node_evaluation max_val_loss NodLink fasttext sum_aggregation reconstruct_node_features node_evaluation nodlink ProGrapher graph2vec textrcnn predict_snapshot_embedding tw_evaluation (or node_evaluation) max_val_loss ThreaTrace only_type sage predict_node_type node_evaluation threatrace OCR-APT ocrapt_features rgcn_per_type one_class node_evaluation ocrapt ShadeWatcher word2vec shadewatcher (TransR + attentive GNN) predict_edge_contrastive (bpr loss) node_evaluation max_val_loss Euler only_type gcn, node_id_embedding, snapshot_gru predict_edge_contrastive (uniform negatives) edge_evaluation max_val_loss Argus only_type argus, node_id_embedding, snapshot_gru predict_edge_contrastive (ap loss) edge_evaluation max_val_loss Jbeil only_type graph_attention, tgn predict_edge_contrastive (tgn negatives) edge_evaluation max_val_loss LARES only_type lares autoencode_edge_embeddings host_two_stage_evaluation k-means on the top host scores E-GraphSAGE only_ones egraphsage predict_edge_contrastive (uniform negatives) edge_evaluation max_val_loss Anomal-E only_ones egraphsage deep_graph_infomax (PCA scores) edge_evaluation max_val_loss

The two families mostly differ at both ends of the pipeline. Most PIDSs embed the textual labels of entities (file paths, command lines, IP addresses), and all are evaluated per node, against the attack nodes of the ground truth. Hosts have no such labels, only a name or an ID, so NIDSs learn an embedding of the identity of each host (node_id_embedding, lares) and rely on the attributes of events; they are evaluated per edge, against the malicious events labelled in the dataset.

Other stages:

  • Transformation. R-Caid builds its pseudo-graph (rcaid_pseudo_graph: the provenance graph plus an edge from each file or socket root to each of its descendants, at most 16 roots per node) and NodLink makes graphs undirected (undirected). Euler, Argus, LARES, E-GraphSAGE and Anomal-E merge the repeated edges of each time window (merge_edges); Argus and LARES aggregate the attributes of the merged events (merge_edges.aggregate_attributes). ShadeWatcher merges them per edge type (merge_edges.per_edge_type), so that each (entity, event type, entity) triple of its knowledge graph is unique.
  • Edge features. Velox, Orthrus and OCR-APT use the edge type; Kairos and Jbeil the TGN messages (msg,time_encoding), which hold the types of the past edges in Kairos (predict_edge_type.edge_type_in_msg); Argus, LARES, E-GraphSAGE and Anomal-E the event attributes (edge_attrs).
  • Epoch selection. PIDSs report the epoch with the best ADP (best_adp, the default). Euler, Jbeil and E-GraphSAGE select it without labels on validation link prediction (best_val_score), Argus and Anomal-E keep the last epoch (last_epoch), and LARES selects the best MCC, as its code. See Choosing the reported epoch.
  • Triage. OCR-APT extracts anomalous subgraphs from its detections (triage.used_method: ocrapt_subgraph).
  • Knowledge graph. ShadeWatcher sees each edge both as an interaction between two entities, scored by the inner product of their embeddings, and as a triple of a knowledge graph whose relation is the edge type. Its encoder adds the loss of TransR on these triples to the BPR loss of the interactions (predict_edge_contrastive with loss: bpr). Entities are embedded from their features (word2vec and type) rather than one embedding per entity, as test entities are mostly unseen during training: add node_id_embedding to the encoders to also learn the identity of each entity.
  • Snapshot-level detection (ProGrapher). ProGrapher embeds each time window as a whole with graph2vec (Weisfeiler-Lehman rooted subgraphs of node and edge types, embedded with doc2vec), and a TextRCNN predicts the embedding of each window from the previous ones (textrcnn.sequence_length): windows far from their prediction are anomalous. Its node scores rank the entities of each window by its key indicators, the rooted subgraphs that explain the deviation the most, so it is evaluated per window as in the paper (tw_evaluation, the default), or per node to compare its key indicators with the other PIDSs (--evaluation.used_method=node_evaluation, optionally with --training.decoder.predict_snapshot_embedding.top_k=4). Its graph2vec model is trained on the train split only; the paper learns the embeddings of all snapshots, test included (--featurization.training_split=all). Its epoch is selected without labels, on the mean prediction error of the validation windows (best_val_score).

The available methods for each column are listed in the reference: Featurization, Encoders, Objectives and Tasks.

items.title: Running across families
items.text:
Datasets are described by a schema (node types, edge types and event attributes) rather than by assumptions on a particular dataset, so a system written for one family runs on the other:

pidsmaker orthrus LANL           # a PIDS on a network dataset
pidsmaker euler CLEARSCOPE_E3    # a NIDS on a provenance dataset

Two differences between the families limit this:

On provenance datasets On network datasets PIDSs All Velox, Orthrus, Kairos, MAGIC, OCR-APT and ShadeWatcher. Flash and ThreaTrace predict node types (predict_node_type), which needs at least two node types, and R-Caid the executables of processes (predict_process_tag): network datasets only have hosts. NodLink is not tested on network datasets. NIDSs Euler and Jbeil as is. Argus, LARES, E-GraphSAGE and Anomal-E use event attributes, which provenance datasets don't have: replace them by the edge type with --batching.edge_features=edge_type. All

The combinations of this table are those run by the tests (tests/test_network_datasets.py). A few useful options when moving across families:

  • --construction.edge_type=logon_type uses a categorical attribute of the events as edge type, e.g. the logon type of LANL authentications as the class predicted by Velox's predict_edge_type.
  • --batching.edge_features=edge_type,edge_attrs gives the event attributes (ports, protocols, logon types...) to a PIDS encoder that reads edge features, such as Orthrus.
  • Systems keep their evaluation: a PIDS on LANL is evaluated per host (node_evaluation, where the malicious hosts are the endpoints of malicious events), a NIDS on CLEARSCOPE_E3 per event (edge_evaluation, where the malicious events are those between attack nodes, with malicious_edge_selection: both_nodes). Switch with evaluation.used_method.

items.title: Variants
items.text:
velox orthrus with the GNN replaced by a single linear layer (training.encoder.used_methods: none) and without TGN neighbor sampling (batching.intra_graph_batching.used_methods: edges). It is the deliberately simple system proposed in Bilot et al.. pretrained_<system> The provenance systems, with node features computed by a pretrained encoder such as SPIDER: pretrained_velox, pretrained_orthrus, pretrained_kairos, pretrained_magic, pretrained_flash, pretrained_nodlink and pretrained_threatrace. cybergfm The CyberGFM baseline: BERT pretrained on random walks, then fine-tuned as a detector with link prediction. --tuned on OPTC_NET The defaults of the network configs are those of LANL. --tuned loads the OpTC settings of LARES (30 min windows, α = 5, β = 30) and Argus (6 min snapshots), from config/tuned_baselines/optc_net/.

Data snooping

Some original configs rely on test data: for example, kairos featurizes nodes using all splits, test included (featurization.training_split: all). PIDSMaker keeps the original configs for reproducibility, except orthrus, which is non-snooped by default for fair comparisons: its word2vec model is trained on the training split only (featurization.training_split: train instead of all), and the k-means clustering after thresholding is disabled. The top of config/orthrus.yml lists the overrides that reproduce the original paper. See Bilot et al. for a detailed analysis.

items.title: Results and reproducibility
items.text:
The default configs contain the original hyperparameters of each system. To find better ones on a dataset, use hyperparameter tuning. Systems trained with self-supervision are unstable, PIDSs and NIDSs alike: always evaluate them over several runs.

Comparing NIDSs with published results

  • The max_val_loss threshold yields almost no true positives on the network datasets: AUC and AP are the meaningful metrics.
  • On OPTC_NET, link prediction on validation edges is close to perfect, so label-free epoch selection picks a nearly arbitrary epoch: report results over several epochs and runs.
  • Euler and Argus evaluate OpTC on another preprocessing and labelling (IP addresses as nodes, all the events of compromised hosts malicious), so their published OpTC results are not comparable with OPTC_NET.

items.title: Adding a system
items.text: Want to add your system? Follow the tutorial to implement it with existing and new components, then open a pull request.

items.title: Tutorial: build a new system
items.text: In this tutorial, we craft a brand new architecture from existing components of the framework and a new encoder, evaluate it on node-level intrusion detection in a provenance dataset, then run it on a network dataset.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
Our goal is to implement a new system that satisfies the following requirements:

  • Compute text embeddings from the textual attributes of entities, such as file paths, process commands, and socket IP addresses.
  • Learn behavior-specific representations for both source and destination nodes.
  • Leverage GraphSAGE layers to capture structural patterns within the provenance graph.
  • Use the node embeddings generated by the encoder as input to a two-layer MLP decoder, training the model in a self-supervised manner to predict edge types—following an approach similar to that of the Kairos and Orthrus systems.
  • In the final step, classify nodes as malicious if their predicted score exceeds a threshold, defined as the maximum loss observed on the validation set.

Approach: we implement a new encoder and integrate it in the framework so that it can be selected from the config. We then write a YAML config describing the pipeline of our system, and run it.

Requirements

  • A GPU with at least 5 GB of memory, or a CPU
  • More than 20 GB of RAM
  • More than 10 GB of storage
  • PIDSMaker installed from source (pip install -e .), as we add files to its code and configs

items.title: 1. Integrate a new encoder
items.text:
In this example, we implement a new encoder that captures whether nodes are source or destination, then uses a GraphSAGE model to capture structural patterns in the provenance graph.

encoders/custom_encoder.py
import torch.nn as nn

from pidsmaker.encoders import SAGE


class CustomEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_dim, hid_dim, out_dim, graph_reindexer, activation, dropout, num_layers, device):
        super().__init__()

        self.src_proj = nn.Linear(in_dim, hid_dim)
        self.dst_proj = nn.Linear(in_dim, hid_dim)

        self.sage = SAGE(
            in_dim=hid_dim,
            hid_dim=hid_dim,
            out_dim=out_dim,
            activation=activation,
            dropout=dropout,
            num_layers=num_layers,
        )

        self.graph_reindexer = graph_reindexer

    def forward(self, x_src, x_dst, edge_index, **kwargs):
        # Project source and destination nodes in a separate embedding space
        h_src = self.src_proj(x_src)  # (E, d)
        h_dst = self.dst_proj(x_dst)  # (E, d)

        # Reshape features to (N, d)
        h_src_N, h_dst_N = self.graph_reindexer.node_features_reshape(edge_index, h_src, h_dst, x_is_tuple=True)
        h = h_src_N + h_dst_N  # (N, d)

        # Pass them through a SAGE GNN
        return self.sage(h, edge_index)

In this example, only two arguments are specific to the encoder and are not shared globally across all encoders: the activation function and the number of GNN layers (num_layers). We want to allow users to specify these parameters via the configuration file to facilitate experimentation with different values. To achieve this, we need to define a new set of arguments tailored specifically for this encoder.

config/config.py
ENCODERS_CFG = {
    ...
    "custom_encoder": {
        "activation": Arg(str),
        "num_layers": Arg(int),
    },
}

Note

If an encoder doesn't rely on any custom arguments, simply leave the dict empty: "custom_encoder": {}, but every encoder should be defined here, or it will not be recognized by the framework.

All logic related to component instantiation is located in factory.py. To integrate our new encoder, we will add a new case in the encoder_factory() function. The existing graph_reindexer instance can be reused. Here, custom_encoder refers to the name of the encoder, which we will later specify in the configuration file.

factory.py: encoder_factory()
    ...
    elif method == "custom_encoder":
        encoder = CustomEncoder(
            in_dim=in_dim,
            hid_dim=node_hid_dim,
            out_dim=node_out_dim,
            dropout=dropout,
            graph_reindexer=graph_reindexer,
            activation=activation_fn_factory(
                cfg.training.encoder.custom_encoder.activation),
            num_layers=cfg.training.encoder.custom_encoder.num_layers,
            device=device,
        )

Our new argument activation can be accessed from the cfg object via cfg.training.encoder.custom_encoder.activation.

Then add the encoder to the list of available encoders in __init__.py.

encoders/__init__.py
...
from .custom_encoder import CustomEncoder

items.title: 2. Integrate a new system
items.text:
To integrate a new system, first create a new YAML file: config/custom_system.yml. This file describes all the logic of the pipeline of our new system. In this example, we take orthrus as base configuration. We only override some arguments for simplicity.

Question

All available arguments for each component and task are listed in the Reference section of the documentation.

Config:

config/custom_system.yml
_include_yml: orthrus # (1)!

construction:
  time_window_size: 15.0 # (2)!
  node_label_features: # (14)!
    subject: type, path, cmd_line
    file: type, path
    netflow: type, remote_ip, remote_port

featurization:
  emb_dim: 128
  epochs: 50
  used_method: word2vec # (15)!
  word2vec:
    alpha: 0.025
    window_size: 5
    min_count: 1
    use_skip_gram: True
    num_workers: 1
    compute_loss: True
    negative: 5
    decline_rate: 30

batching:
  node_features: node_emb,node_type # (16)!
  edge_features: none # (17)!
  intra_graph_batching:
    used_methods: none # (3)!

training:
  lr: 0.0001 # (4)!
  node_hid_dim: 128
  node_out_dim: 128

  encoder:
    dropout: 0.3
    used_methods: custom_encoder # (5)!
    custom_encoder:
      activation: relu # (6)!
      num_layers: 3

  decoder:
    used_methods: predict_edge_type # (7)!
    predict_edge_type:
      decoder: edge_mlp # (8)!
      edge_mlp:
        src_dst_projection_coef: 2 # (9)!
        architecture_str: linear(0.5) | relu # (10)!

evaluation:
  used_method: node_evaluation # (11)!
  node_evaluation:
    threshold_method: max_val_loss # (12)!
    use_kmeans: False # (13)!
  1. In this example, we take the orthrus system as base configuration.
  2. We partition the graphs in time windows of size 15 minutes.
  3. By default orthrus partitions each time window in even smaller batches of 1024 edges. To discard this behavior, we set used_methods: None.
  4. We set some custom hyperparameters for training.
  5. It's here that we tell the encoder to use, in this case our new custom_encoder.
  6. We set the values for our two defined arguments: activation and num_layers.
  7. Our objective is to predict edge types as recent research shows it is the best approach yet.
  8. Here, edge_mlp is a MLP designed for edge-level tasks like edge type prediction. It first projects src and dst nodes with different linear layers, then applies the MLP specified in architecture_str.
  9. This arg refers to how many times the size of the input should be the output of the src/dst linear layer. Here we want to project to an embedding with double the input size.
  10. Our final neural network prior to prediction is a two-layer MLP including relu activation. An additional linear layer is added after the relu to match the output size expected by the objective, here the number of edge types.
  11. Refers to node-level detection.
  12. We compute the threshold based on the maximum loss seen on the validation set.
  13. We use here a simple thresholding, without clustering.
  14. We describe here the features assigned to each type of entity.
  15. We train a word2vec model and embed each node's features (node_label_features) into a vector of size emb_dim.
  16. The features to use as node features during GNN training. Here we concatenate the word2vec embedding and one-hot encoded entity type.
  17. Our model doesn't integrate edge features so we do not use any in this example.

items.title: 3. Run the pipeline
items.text:
You can now run the pipeline. With the editable install, your changes to the code are used without reinstalling.

For tiny experiments, you can run the framework locally like so:

pidsmaker custom_system CADETS_E3 --project=test_custom_system

For more practical experimentation, prefer running the framework in background and monitor the logs, figures and metrics in Weights & Biases (W&B). To do so, ensure you have logged to W&B with wandb login and run:

pidsmaker custom_system CADETS_E3 --wandb --background --project=test_custom_system

Note

Use --cpu to run the framework on CPU instead of GPU.

items.title: 4. Analyze the results
items.text:
In the W&B interface, go to the test_custom_system project and you can check real-time logs and metrics being updated to your ongoing run.

Once finished, we provide some figures to illustrate the ability of the model to differentiate attack and benign nodes.

Results show a noticeable separation between benign and some malicious nodes on all three attacks in the E3-CADETS dataset. However, the threshold (vertical line) is not adequately located in the space of anomaly scores, leading to 21 TPs and 33 FPs, whereas some nodes can be detected without any FP.

System metrics such as GPU memory, RAM, and CPU utilization are automatically captured by W&B and can be visualized on the interface.

items.title: 5. Try variants
items.text:
While this first version of the model yields relatively satisfactory results, we have no guarantee it has the best performing set of arguments on this dataset. We can easily experiment with multiple variants using CLI args. Depending on your hardware, you can run multiple runs in parallel even on a single GPU (usually up to 3-4 parallel runs with simple architectures on a A100 GPU without major runtime overhead).

# Remove node type from node features, keep only the word2vec embedding
pidsmaker custom_system CADETS_E3 --wandb --background --project=test_custom_system \
    --batching.node_features=node_emb

# Increase node embedding size
pidsmaker custom_system CADETS_E3 --wandb --background --project=test_custom_system \
    --training.node_hid_dim=256 \
    --training.node_out_dim=256

# Reduce the number of GNN layers
pidsmaker custom_system CADETS_E3 --wandb --background --project=test_custom_system \
    --training.encoder.custom_encoder.num_layers=2

For more advanced hyperparameter exploration, consider using the hyperparameter tuning feature.

items.title: 6. Run it on network data
items.text:
Nothing in our system is specific to provenance: the encoder only sees node features and edges, and the objective predicts edge types. The same config runs on a network dataset, whose nodes are hosts and edges authentications:

pidsmaker custom_system LANL --wandb --background --project=test_custom_system \
    --construction.edge_type=logon_type

Here, the decoder predicts the logon type of each authentication (Network, Interactive, RemoteInteractive...) instead of a system call, and node_evaluation scores hosts, whose ground truth is the endpoints of the red team's authentications. To evaluate each authentication instead, as the network systems do, add --evaluation.used_method=edge_evaluation.

Host names carry little information for word2vec, unlike file paths and command lines: network systems instead learn the identity of each host and use the attributes of events. See how they are built in Systems, and the Pipeline for the differences between both kinds of data at each stage.

items.title: Cleaning
items.text:
The databases of the datasets contain events and attributes that are artifacts of the collection rather than system behavior: null values stored as text, corrupted IPs, events logged twice, events of a process on itself, multicast name resolution traffic, etc. They are cleaned during the construction task, before the graphs are built, with construction.cleaning.

The cleaning methods were designed for provenance datasets. On network datasets, the methods that filter events (remove_duplicate_events, remove_self_loops, dedup_window_edges) apply to the events between hosts: E-GraphSAGE and Anomal-E remove self-loops. remove_noisy_netflows only applies to the netflow nodes of provenance datasets; the broadcast and multicast flows of OPTC_NET are dropped by construction.drop_noise_events instead.

used_methods is a comma-separated list of methods, or none. The default none builds the same graphs as the original systems, and keeps reusing the graphs already built.

Method Effect Removes nodes remove_null_attributes Null-like attribute values (None, NA, null, unknown, <UNNAMED fd:3>, IPs that do not parse, ports outside 1-65535) are removed from node labels instead of becoming tokens such as None no normalize_labels Trims labels, collapses whitespaces and repeated slashes, removes Windows path prefixes (\\?\, //?/) and quotes, optionally lowercases, and truncates labels longer than max_length characters no remove_duplicate_events Events with the same source, destination, type and timestamp are kept once no remove_self_loops Events from a node to itself are removed only nodes without other events remove_noisy_netflows Netflow nodes whose remote IP is in ip_categories (multicast and 255.255.255.255 by default) are removed with their events yes dedup_window_edges Only the first event of each (source, destination, type) is kept in each time window graph no

For example, Velox with the methods that do not remove attack nodes on any dataset:

pidsmaker velox CADETS_E3 \
  --construction.cleaning.used_methods=remove_null_attributes,normalize_labels,remove_duplicate_events,remove_self_loops

construction:
  cleaning:
    used_methods: remove_null_attributes, normalize_labels, remove_duplicate_events, remove_self_loops
    normalize_labels:
      collapse_whitespace: True
      collapse_slashes: True
      strip_path_prefixes: True
      strip_quotes: True
      lowercase: False
      max_length: 512
    remove_noisy_netflows:
      ip_categories: multicast, broadcast

The order of the methods has no effect. The construction folder only depends on the arguments of the used methods.

items.title: What is cleaned in each dataset
items.text:
The methods come from a profiling of the databases and of the graphs built from them.

  • Null values stored as text. Node attributes that are missing in the database are stored as None, so that 98% of the files of CADETS_E3 are labeled file None. Netflows of ClearScope E3 have the IP 0 or <UNNAMED fd:N>, those of ClearScope E5 None, those of Theia E3 NA, and those of Trace E3 hexadecimal characters such as E and D as remote IP. remove_null_attributes removes them from the labels.
  • Label formatting. Command lines of Theia contain runs of spaces (/bin/sh -c cd /), paths contain repeated slashes (/var/lib/apt//lists/), Windows paths are prefixed (//?/C:/Program Files/...) or quoted, and some command lines reach 40,000 characters (Trace E3). normalize_labels gives the same label to these variants.
  • Duplicated events. 2% (ATLASv2) to 55% (CADETS E3) of the events have the same source, destination, type and timestamp as another event. fuse_edge already merges most of them, but not with fuse_edge: False. Event UUIDs cannot be used to find duplicates: CADETS reuses them for unrelated events.
  • Self-loops. ClearScope logs reads of processes on themselves (17,000 edges in the graphs of ClearScope E3, 60,000 in E5) and OpTC logs TERMINATE and OPEN events of processes on themselves (93,000 edges in OpTC h201).
  • Multicast traffic. In OpTC h201, 3.1 of the 3.4 million netflow nodes are multicast name resolution (LLMNR, SSDP) to 224.0.0.252, ff02::1:3 or 239.255.255.250.
  • Repeated events in a time window. After fuse_edge, 20% (CADETS E3) to 73% (ClearScope E5) of the edges of a graph repeat the source, destination and type of an earlier edge of the same graph, e.g. reads of /dev/ashmem. dedup_window_edges keeps one of them. Encoders that use the order and number of events (e.g. TGN) lose this information.

items.title: Effect on detection
items.text:
Cleaning changes the input of the systems, so its effect depends on the system. Best ADP of single runs (seed 0) on CADETS_E3:

Cleaning Velox Velox with SPIDER none 0.62 1.0 remove_null_attributes 0.97 0.62 normalize_labels 0.62 1.0 remove_duplicate_events 0.34 0.91 remove_self_loops 0.63 1.0 remove_noisy_netflows 0.62 1.0 dedup_window_edges 0.68 0.70 all methods 1.0 0.77

And of Velox on other datasets:

Dataset none all methods THEIA_E3 0.79 0.80 CLEARSCOPE_E3 0.01 0.25 optc_h201 0.12 0.33 (7 attack nodes removed)
  • remove_null_attributes helps featurization methods learned on the dataset: all processes of CADETS have a null path, so with none the token None is in the label of every process (subject None sleep).
  • Pretrained encoders such as SPIDER were pretrained on labels that were not cleaned: methods that change the labels or the events change their input, and lower their results.
  • normalize_labels, remove_self_loops and remove_noisy_netflows have no effect on CADETS_E3, which has few such labels and events.

As detectors are unstable (see Instability), measure the effect of cleaning on several runs before using it.

items.title: Attack nodes
items.text:
Methods that remove nodes can remove attack nodes, which are then not evaluated. The construction task writes cleaning_report.json in its folder, with the number of events and nodes removed by each method and ground_truth_nodes_lost, the number of attack nodes of the ground truth that are not in the graphs anymore. The ground truth is only read to write this report: it has no effect on cleaning.

remove_noisy_netflows is the only method that removed attack nodes in our datasets: 7 multicast netflow nodes in OpTC h201.

items.title: Command line
items.text:
The pidsmaker command is the single entry point of the framework: it runs a system on a dataset, and downloads datasets. Besides the task arguments, a run accepts the flags below, which control how it is executed rather than what it computes.

pidsmaker SYSTEM DATASET [FLAGS] [--task.argument=value ...]

From a clone of the repository, python pidsmaker/main.py SYSTEM DATASET ... is equivalent.

Positional Description SYSTEM Name of a YAML config in config/, without the extension (e.g. velox, pretrained_velox, euler). See Systems. DATASET Name of a dataset in DATASET_DEFAULT_CONFIG (e.g. CADETS_E3, optc_h201, LANL, OPTC_NET). See Datasets.

Any argument from the Reference can be passed as --task.argument=value; it overrides the YAML config.

items.title: Pipeline control
items.text: Flag Default Description --force_restart TASK Re-runs the pipeline from TASK (e.g. featurization), overwriting the cached outputs. See Forcing a restart. --restart_from_scratch off Runs every task in a new folder with a random hash. Its outputs are deleted at the end of the run. --cpu off Runs on CPU even if a GPU is available. --save_for_viz off Keeps the per-epoch checkpoints and test graphs needed by the embedding visualizer. --save_graph_preprocessing off Saves the preprocessed graphs on disk (heavy).

items.title: Performance
items.text:
These flags don't change the results, nor the task hashes. See Performance and Disk usage.

Flag Default Description --num_workers N min(8, #CPUs) Number of processes for CPU-bound preprocessing such as graph construction. --no_shared_node_features off Stores node features per batch instead of in a shared table rebuilt for each batch. Uses much more memory; for debugging. --keep_best_epoch_only off At the end of the pipeline, deletes the loss files, evaluation pickles and weights of all epochs except the best one (stats and plots are kept). Re-running evaluation afterwards only considers the kept epoch.

items.title: Experiment tracking
items.text: Flag Default Description --wandb off Sends logs, metrics and figures to Weights & Biases. --project NAME PIDSMaker W&B project of the run. --exp NAME Name of the experiment, to group and find runs in W&B. --tags TAGS W&B tags of the run.

items.title: Experiments and tuning
items.text: Flag Default Description --experiment NAME none Runs an experiment defined in config/experiments/uncertainty/, e.g. run_n_times to measure instability. --tuning_mode MODE none hyperparameters starts a W&B sweep. See Hyperparameter tuning. --tuning_file_path PATH Sweep config to use instead of the dataset-specific one, relative to config/experiments/tuning/ (e.g. systems/default/tuning_my_system). --sweep_id ID Joins an existing W&B sweep, to run it with several agents. --tuned off Loads the tuned hyperparameters of the system from config/tuned_baselines/<dataset>/tuned_<system>.yml (e.g. LARES and Argus on OPTC_NET).

items.title: Datasets and storage
items.text: Flag Default Description --datasets_dir PATH $PIDSMAKER_DATASETS_DIR, else ~/.cache/pidsmaker/datasets Folder of the Parquet datasets, one subfolder per dataset. --artifact_dir PATH $PIDSMAKER_ARTIFACT_DIR, else /home/artifacts/ if it exists, else ./artifacts/ Folder where all task outputs are written.

items.title: Downloading datasets
items.text:
pidsmaker download downloads datasets from Hugging Face (see Download the datasets):

pidsmaker download DATASET [DATASET ...]   # or `all`
pidsmaker download --list                  # the datasets, their sizes, and which are downloaded

Dataset names are case-insensitive, and the names of their databases work too (e.g. optc_051 for optc_h051). Datasets already downloaded are skipped, and interrupted downloads resume where they stopped.

Flag Default Description --list Lists the datasets, their sizes, and which are downloaded. --datasets_dir PATH $PIDSMAKER_DATASETS_DIR, else ~/.cache/pidsmaker/datasets Where datasets are stored. --repo REPO $PIDSMAKER_HF_REPO, else pidsmaker/datasets Hugging Face dataset repository. --revision REVISION Branch, tag or commit of the repository. --force off Downloads the datasets again, even if they are already downloaded.

The same from Python: from pidsmaker.datasets import download; download("CADETS_E3").

items.title: Environment variables
items.text: Variable Default Description PIDSMAKER_DATASETS_DIR ~/.cache/pidsmaker/datasets Folder of the datasets (default of --datasets_dir). PIDSMAKER_ARTIFACT_DIR /home/artifacts/ if it exists, else ./artifacts/ Folder of the artifacts (default of --artifact_dir). PIDSMAKER_AUTO_DOWNLOAD 1 A run downloads its dataset if it is missing. With 0, it stops with an error instead. PIDSMAKER_HF_REPO pidsmaker/datasets Hugging Face dataset repository of the datasets (default of --repo). PIDSMAKER_DUCKDB_THREADS 8 Threads of each DuckDB connection. Graph construction opens several connections at the same time, one per day. OMP_NUM_THREADS CPU threads of PyTorch (by default, one per core).

items.title: Running in the background
items.text:
--background runs the pipeline detached from the terminal: the run continues after you close it or log out, and its output goes to a log file in the current folder, pidsmaker_SYSTEM_DATASET_<time>.log, whose path the command prints. Several runs can be started in parallel this way.

pidsmaker orthrus CADETS_E3 --wandb --background

To run a system on several datasets one after the other, in the background:

nohup sh -c 'for d in CLEARSCOPE_E3 CADETS_E3 THEIA_E3; do pidsmaker SYSTEM $d --wandb --restart_from_scratch; done' > runs.log 2>&1 &

items.title: Reproducibility
items.text: pidsmaker runs the pipeline with PYTHONHASHSEED=0, so that sets of strings are iterated in the same order in every run, and CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8, needed by the deterministic algorithms of CUDA (training.deterministic). Values you set yourself are kept. python pidsmaker/main.py runs without them.

items.title: Decoders
items.text:
Decoders take as input node and/or edge embeddings and pass them through another neural network in such a way that the last layer has a shape that fits the downstream objective. For example, a predict_edge_type objective requires the final shape to be the number of edge types, whereas a reconstruct_node_features objective needs a shape that matches the input features given to the encoder. Decoders are usually much simpler than encoders, and can be customized via edge_mlp for edge-level tasks like predict_edge_type or via node_mlp for node-level tasks like reconstruct_node_features.

The autoencode_edge_embeddings and deep_graph_infomax objectives don't use a decoder (decoder: none): they have their own networks.

Example: if the encoder's output has shape node_out_dim=128 setting architecture_str=linear(2) | relu | linear(0.5) creates this MLP: nn.Linear(128, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 128), nn.Linear(128, y). Precisely, in linear(x), x is the multiplier of input neurons. dropout(p) adds a dropout of rate p, dropout one of rate training.encoder.dropout. The final layer nn.Linear(128, y) is added automatically such that y is the output size matching the downstream objective (e.g. edge type prediction involves predicting 10 edge types, so the output of the decoder should be 10).
